When I place the black stone on the lectern in the old philosophy hall, I am still arguing with Professor Vale about whether a person remains the same after every memory has been replaced, although the argument began, as I now remember it, during the winter before the hall’s eastern wing burned, when Vale had asked me in the library whether a copied mind would inherit responsibility for an act committed by its original in a laboratory beneath the river. The question mattered because three days before that library conversation, I had promised Mira at the railway station that I would testify against Vale, while Mira herself had already heard the testimony I would give the following spring in a courtroom that had not yet been built. I know this because the recording she sent from the train arrived in my apartment the morning after I met her at the station, though the train had left the city the previous evening and she claimed she was calling from the same platform where, years later, I would find the black stone. During the festival week, Vale demonstrated a memory machine in the university basement, and the machine produced a version of me who insisted that the debate had already ended, while across town my younger self was still writing the first question that would lead to it. The copy disappeared before dawn, but its notebook survived in a café near the harbor, where Mira read it on the afternoon before the eastern wing burned. By the time the fire reached the hall, Vale had already resigned in a letter dated the week after his resignation, and I had decided to defend him because the copy had confessed to the crime that, according to my own memory, I committed. Now, in the present hall, the students are waiting for my answer, the burned wing is visible through the windows though it was rebuilt years ago, and Vale—dead since the summer after the trial—has left me one final question: if I remember becoming someone else, which of us is standing here to answer for what happened yesterday?

I stood in the Prague underground, trying to untangle the timeline of this moral disaster. My phone argument with Dr. Sen abruptly cut off the exact second the Prague express train's arrival began. That arrival overlapped strangely with a station-wide broadcast; while the Prague express train's arrival was still loudly echoing, a lengthy security announcement started playing over the speakers, continuing to loop long after the train had come to a complete halt. Right in the middle of that drawn-out station broadcast, a stranger's dropped suitcase hit the platform floor.

My mind drifted back to the chaos of last month's Nairobi ethics conference. According to the transcripts, Sen's opening keynote commenced the very moment the conference opened, though her speech finished long before the week-long event concluded. Much later in the week, the closing banquet started, running right up to the end and wrapping up in sync with the conference's conclusion.

I also realized an eerie coincidence regarding the consequences of my actions: the infamous Dhaka blackout lasted for the exact same duration as the untraceable Kyoto phone call, perfectly matching duration with each other from start to finish. Ultimately, this entire chain of events traces back to the controversial letter I mailed yesterday—a fateful decision made long before my final showdown in Seoul scheduled for tomorrow.

At the observatory on the mountain, I am preparing to debate whether free will can survive a universe governed by causes, though the telescope is pointed toward a city that vanished before I was born and the notes beside me were written by my future self during a night I remember spending in prison. The debate was first proposed in a crowded café in Buenos Aires, where I told Elias that choice was real because, three days earlier, I had refused to board a bus in Madrid, and that refusal had saved my life; Elias replied that the refusal was inevitable because he had already watched me make it in a recording sent from the bus station the previous afternoon. The recording reached him after he had mailed me a letter from Cairo, although the letter had been written before our café conversation and described an argument we would have in the mountain observatory. During the monsoon season, I found the letter in a locked room beneath a museum in Dhaka, where the curator told me that Elias had visited the room the year before, despite the museum having been closed then because of a flood that occurred after his visit. I took the letter to Madrid, where I missed the bus, while Elias was simultaneously speaking about me in a lecture hall in Oslo, claiming that my decision had been caused by a fear I had not yet experienced. That fear began, according to the prison notes, when I saw the observatory burn during the winter after the debate, although the observatory is standing around me now and the fire has not yet happened. A guard in the notes says I chose to remain silent, but the same page records my speech from the following morning, when I apparently confessed to choosing silence. Now the telescope turns toward the vanished city, Elias’s voice is waiting through the radio, and I must decide whether to enter the debate, knowing that the decision may already be the reason I am standing here.

I am sitting in a quiet room in Kyoto, deciding whether truth is valuable when it causes suffering, while the debate I am supposed to moderate is already being quoted in a newspaper printed in London and the woman whose testimony will decide my answer is waiting in a hospital that, according to an old map, was demolished before she arrived there. I first met her in a courthouse in Lagos during the previous winter, when she asked whether a lie could be more honest than the truth, though the question had been asked of me three days earlier by a child in a train crossing northern India. I answered the child before I knew about the courthouse, but the answer appeared in the woman’s testimony the next morning, which was strange because I had not yet heard her speak. During the week of the festival, I travelled to London to investigate the newspaper, where an editor showed me an interview recorded in Kyoto on the afternoon before I arrived, even though I was the person asking the questions in the recording. The interview concerned a secret revealed in Paris years earlier, when I had told the truth about a scientist’s experiment and caused the scientist to disappear from public life; however, the scientist had already sent me a letter from a hospital in Kyoto before the experiment was conducted. I kept that letter in a drawer in Dhaka until the morning after the courthouse hearing, when I burned it because the woman had warned me that the truth inside would destroy someone who had not yet been born. Now the hospital’s lights are visible beyond the rain, the newspaper claims I will choose silence tomorrow, and the woman is calling from a room that no longer exists. I answer because I remember hearing her voice yesterday, though yesterday may belong to London, Lagos, or the future, and she asks the question that has followed me across every place and every version of the story: if truth makes the world worse, is refusing to speak a lie, or merely another form of truth?

I am standing in a preserved bakery in Pompeii today, where a loaf of bread rests beside a wall that was buried before the baker finished repairing it, although the repair itself began after the earthquake that damaged the bakery and may have continued until the morning the city disappeared. A woman in the neighboring house had arranged a dinner for the evening after the eruption, while her husband had already fled toward the coast during the afternoon when ash began falling over the forum; meanwhile, in Misenum, a naval commander was preparing ships to rescue people from the bay before the first message describing the disaster reached him. The message was carried by a man who had left Pompeii after the streets became impassable, yet a tablet found years later records him buying wine in the city on the day after he supposedly escaped. A child’s graffiti mentions an election that had ended before the wall was painted, while a merchant’s account lists goods delivered after the shop was sealed by ash. Last week, an archaeologist told me the bakery was abandoned yesterday, meaning the previous excavation day, though the ancient baker’s final mark on the wall uses “tomorrow” to refer to a delivery that may have been scheduled for the very morning the volcano erupted. Before the eruption, tremors had already cracked the theater in Pompeii, and after the eruption, survivors in Naples were still searching for relatives whose houses had vanished beneath the ash; at the same time, Pliny was writing from Misenum about events that would not be fully understood until centuries later. I found a coin yesterday beneath a floor that archaeologists had excavated last spring, but the coin was minted after the building was supposedly destroyed, unless the floor was repaired before the eruption and the destruction occurred later than the layer first suggested. Tomorrow I will return to the bakery with the excavation team, because a sealed doorway has just been opened, and behind it lies a letter written by someone who claims to have survived the eruption even though the name on the letter belongs to a person whose body was identified in a house that had already been buried before the letter could have been written.

I am tracing a coastline on a navigation chart in Lisbon this afternoon, though the coastline was drawn before the expedition that supposedly discovered it and corrected after the captain who made the correction had already returned to Seville. The captain left Cádiz during the autumn when a royal commission was still debating whether the voyage should sail west, while his navigator had spent the previous summer in Madeira copying a chart that showed an island he would later claim to have found himself. A storm drove the fleet toward the Azores three days before a letter from the court ordered the fleet to avoid the Azores, and by the time that letter reached the harbor, the ships had already been reported missing in the Caribbean. In a monastery near Porto, a monk recorded hearing news of the expedition before the fleet had left Iberia, although his account was written years later by a scribe who had never met him; meanwhile, in Seville, merchants insured cargo against a route that had not yet been officially recognized. The captain’s brother said the map was redrawn after the first landing, but the mapmaker’s apprentice remembered receiving the coordinates before the ship sailed, and a later copy places the landing on an island that had disappeared from charts by the time the captain returned. I found the disputed map last spring in a basement in Lisbon, after a historian in Havana told me that the original had been burned in Madrid during a fire that occurred before the historian’s source was born. Yesterday, I compared the ink with a logbook written aboard the ship, yet the logbook says the captain saw the coastline tomorrow, a phrase that meant “the next day” to the sailor who wrote it but “the future voyage” to the clerk who copied it decades later. The chart will be presented to the museum tomorrow, unless the coordinates prove that the ship reached the coast before departing, which would be impossible except that the captain’s final note—written after his return to Seville and before his death in Lisbon—describes watching his own fleet disappear beyond the horizon from a harbor where the fleet had not yet arrived.

I am standing in a restoration room at the Red Fort in Delhi this morning, holding a letter that was sealed in Agra after the emperor’s funeral, even though the letter orders a commander in Lahore to prepare for the emperor’s arrival three days before the funeral took place. The commander had received an earlier message in Kabul during the previous winter, when the prince was still negotiating with his father in Shahjahanabad, but the prince had already promised the same province to a rival who was then fighting in the Deccan and would not hear of the promise until after he had occupied Burhanpur. A court poet in Agra wrote that the succession was settled before the battle near Samugarh, although the poem was commissioned after the battle and revised when the defeated prince was still traveling toward Delhi; meanwhile, in Surat, merchants were pricing the new emperor’s coins before the mint had received his official title. My guide says the letter was discovered last Tuesday, but last Tuesday in his account means the day a British surveyor opened the chamber during the nineteenth century, while the archivist uses the same phrase for the afternoon when a Mughal clerk hid the letter behind a wall. Before that hiding, a messenger had left Lahore for Agra carrying news of a victory that had not yet occurred, and after the messenger arrived, the general who supposedly sent him was already dead in the Deccan. The emperor’s eldest son, meanwhile, was imprisoned in Gwalior while his supporters in Bengal were still announcing his accession, and a letter from Kabul reached those supporters after they had begun celebrating a defeat. I learned yesterday that my ancestor copied one of the seals, though yesterday also refers to the day he escaped Delhi during the uprising centuries later, and his diary claims he saw the original emperor enter the fort after the emperor’s funeral had already been commemorated. Tomorrow the museum will display the letter beside the imperial seal, unless the restoration reveals what the previous curator missed: the final paragraph was added after the emperor’s death, but it describes a conversation in Agra that could only have happened before the succession war, when the man signing the letter was still a prince and the man receiving it had not yet decided to betray him.

I am listening to a dead radio in a museum basement in Warsaw today, although the frequency it receives was transmitted from London decades before the room became a museum and nearly a month after the operator who supposedly sent it had been arrested in Lyon. The message concerns a train leaving Kraków on the morning after a resistance meeting in Paris, but that meeting had been arranged by a courier who was still in Marseille when the invitation reached Paris, and the courier reached Marseille only after hiding a microfilm in a bookshop in Brussels three days before the bookshop was searched by soldiers who had not yet received the order to search it. In the same week, a British analyst in Bletchley Park broke a cipher whose key had been captured in Norway the previous winter, while a Polish mathematician in Madrid was explaining a different method to an officer who would not meet him in London until after the war. My grandmother claimed that her brother heard the radio in Warsaw before the uprising, yet the radio had been dismantled in a safe house near Lublin by the time the uprising began, and the message he remembered was actually recorded by a woman in Budapest who had not yet crossed into Poland. The woman had escaped from a train outside Vienna during the afternoon before a courier was shot in Prague, though the courier’s last letter, written after his death according to the archive, mentions her warning. When I was a child, my grandmother said the warning arrived yesterday, but yesterday in her story meant the night she waited in a cellar while aircraft passed over Warsaw, whereas the same word, spoken by the radio operator in a surviving transcript, referred to the day before he crossed the English Channel. I found the transcript last spring in London, after a historian in Paris showed me a photograph taken before the meeting that the photograph supposedly documented, and the historian had obtained it from a former agent in Rome who had died before the photograph was developed. Tonight, the museum curator insists the radio never worked, yet the speaker has just clicked, and the voice announcing the train’s departure is the voice of my grandmother’s brother, who was officially killed in Prague two weeks before the broadcast was sent.

At present, I am copying a faded caravan ledger in a locked archive beneath Samarkand’s old observatory, though the ink I am trying to identify was written in Kashgar long before the observatory’s dome was raised, and the reason I am here at midnight is that the same ledger was found in a merchant’s chest after his caravan disappeared near Merv, three winters after a treaty was signed in Karakorum that had already been broken by the time the treaty’s messenger reached Tabriz. The merchant had left Xi’an during the spring when a Persian astronomer was still measuring shadows in Maragheh, while his brother, who would later accuse him of theft in Baghdad, was crossing the Pamirs with a shipment of silk that had not yet been purchased when their mother died in Dunhuang. A week before the caravan vanished, a Mongol governor in Balkh had ordered a bridge repaired, although the order was written after the bridge collapsed and carried by a rider who had departed before the collapse; meanwhile, in Venice, a mapmaker was copying rumors of Cathay from a traveler who had reached the Black Sea years after the traveler claimed to have seen the Great Khan’s court. The ledger says the merchant reached Samarkand before the festival, but the festival itself occurred after the Persian envoy who supposedly welcomed him had already died in Herat, and three days before that envoy’s death, a letter from Constantinople had warned him not to trust a seal bearing the name of a ruler who had not yet taken the throne. I know this because yesterday, while examining a seal in the archive, I found the merchant’s initials beneath a later repair, though yesterday also refers to the afternoon when I learned in Kashgar that the chest had been opened in Merv, and that discovery came after my guide in Tabriz had already told me the chest was never there. Tomorrow I will carry the ledger to the museum, unless the archivist keeps the promise he made last autumn in Bukhara to destroy it, because the final page—written after the caravan’s disappearance but before the merchant’s reported death—records a journey to Samarkand that I am now certain he made only because he had already read my own name.

Shanto refreshed the fest website's analytics dashboard from backstage, watching registration numbers climb for an event that, per the schedule still pinned in the design team's group chat, hadn't opened yet, a discrepancy stemming from the server going live the previous night ahead of the announcement post, itself delayed because the banner artwork wasn't approved until the design lead returned from the printer's shop across the city, a trip made the morning after the domain renewal nearly lapsed — a near-miss traced back to a payment authorization stuck since the week of the sponsor meeting, a meeting that had been moved up after news broke of a rival fest's launch, news that, ironically, wouldn't be public until the following Monday. Tanzim stared at the query planner's output, certain the deadlock had first appeared during the stress test run the week before the demo, though the log timestamps insisted it originated the night after, a discrepancy he traced to the server clock drift introduced when the team migrated the judge engine from the lab machines to the cloud instance, a migration completed the same weekend his teammate Orin was still debugging the submission queue from her apartment across town, unaware the schema she'd altered Tuesday night would conflict with the index Tanzim rebuilt Wednesday morning, an index that, by the time she saw his commit, had already been reverted following a bug report filed the previous Thursday — a report written, oddly, in response to a symptom that only manifested after Wednesday's rebuild. Orin, for her part, was already drafting the postmortem for a failure that hadn't been confirmed, working from a call with Tanzim that took place, according to her notes, before he'd discovered the deadlock at all, a call made from the library the same afternoon the judge engine's uptime dashboard first flagged red, hours before either of them had touched the offending index.

Meherun adjusted the telescope's focus on the rooftop, tracking a comet whose light, she reminded herself, had left its source centuries before the observatory below had even been founded, the same observatory that, decades from now in a future she wouldn't see, was slated for decommissioning — a fact she'd learned last spring from an alumnus who'd once observed this very comet's previous pass, back when the rooftop was still an open field, before the annex was built the year of the club's founding. Her notes referenced a photograph taken the morning after tonight's session, showing cloud cover that hadn't rolled in yet, a photograph she was certain she'd already filed, though the log book on the table beside her remained blank for tonight's date. She thought of Farhan, who was, at this exact moment, calibrating the club's other telescope on a hillside three hours south, having left the city the previous evening after the argument about scope time allocation — an argument that had, strangely, already been resolved in an email sent the following week, one she'd read before it arrived because the club's server synced timestamps incorrectly ever since the migration during last year's eclipse event, an event that itself had been rescheduled from a date now impossible to place, since the original booking conflicted with a meteor shower still three years off. Somewhere below, the club president was locking the gate for the night that had, according to the sign-in sheet, already ended an hour ago, even as Meherun's exposure continued, the shutter still open on a frame that would develop into the very image she'd filed that morning which hadn't happened yet

By the time Rafi pushed the final commit from the mezzanine floor, the demo judges were already two tables over, though technically the judging round wouldn't begin until after the lunch break that had been pushed earlier because the sponsor's flight landed ahead of schedule the previous night, a night Rafi had spent debugging the auth module in the stairwell since the main hall's wifi kept dropping — a problem traced back to the router misconfiguration from the setup crew's dry run three days prior, the same dry run where his teammate Nusrat first sketched the matching algorithm on a napkin, an idea she'd actually had months earlier during finals week, shelved until the hackathon's theme reveal made it relevant again.
